title: Sickle Cell Anemia
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Sickle cell anemia is a homozygous β‑globin mutation (βs/βs) causing HbS >80% of total hemoglobin. The valine‑for‑glutamic‑acid substitution makes red cells sickle, leading to chronic hemolysis, vaso‑occlusion and multi‑system complications.

sections.p: A single point mutation (GAG → GTG) in the β‑globin gene replaces glutamic acid with valine at codon 6. Homozygous individuals produce mostly HbS, which polymerises when deoxygenated, distorting red cells.
b: Autosomal recessive inheritance
Prevalence high in East Africa, especially among Nilotic and Bantu groups
Chronic hemolytic anemia with episodic vaso‑occlusive crises

sections.p: Normal hemoglobin (HbA) remains soluble in both oxygenated and deoxygenated states. HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, causing red cells to become rigid, sticky and sickle‑shaped, impairing microvascular flow.
b: Polymerisation threshold reached when HbS >30% and oxygen tension falls
Sickled cells have reduced deformability and increased adhesion to endothelium
Rapid removal by spleen → hemolysis

sections.p: Erythropoiesis is driven by hypoxia‑induced erythropoietin; chronic hemolysis stimulates marrow expansion, leading to bone pain and skeletal changes.
b: Elevated reticulocyte count (>5%) reflects marrow response
Increased fetal hemoglobin (HbF) mitigates sickling; hydroxyurea raises HbF

sections.p: Polymerised HbS deforms red cells, causing hemolysis and vaso‑occlusion. Repeated infarctions damage organs; splenic autoinfarction leads to functional asplenia and infection risk.
b: Acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration, priapism
Secondary iron overload from transfusions
Increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria

sections.p: Patients present with chronic anemia, jaundice, and painful crises. In low‑resource settings, malaria, HIV, TB and limited transfusion services worsen outcomes.
b: Pain crisis triggered by dehydration, infection, cold, high altitude
Severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL) may need transfusion
Splenic sequestration: sudden splenomegaly, drop in Hb >2 g/dL

t.b: Confirms diagnosis; HbS >80% indicates homozygous disease
Shows normocytic anemia, reticulocytosis; if unavailable, peripheral smear with sickle cells is supportive
Elevated in chronic hemolysis; helps differentiate from hepatic jaundice

t.a: Chest X‑ray (if acute chest syndrome suspected)
t.b: Detects new infiltrates; if radiology not available, rely on fever, cough, hypoxia
Screens for stroke risk; if unavailable, use clinical risk factors (previous stroke, severe anemia)

sections.p: Treat acute crises, prevent complications, and modify disease biology.
b: Hydration and analgesia for vaso‑occlusive pain; avoid NSAIDs if renal risk
Oxygen for hypoxia; simple transfusion for Hb <7 g/dL or acute chest syndrome
Hydroxyurea (if available) to raise HbF and reduce crises
Penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination for asplenic patients
Iron chelation (e.g., deferasirox) for transfusion‑related iron overload

sections.p: Conditions that cause hemolytic anemia or painful crises.
b: G6PD deficiency – episodic hemolysis after oxidative stress, no sickle cells
Thalassemia major – microcytic anemia, target cells, not sickling
Sickle‑cell trait (HbAS) – usually asymptomatic, occasional hematuria

sections.p: Laboratory and clinical findings that may be falsely reassuring.
b: Low HbS percentage in a recent transfusion may mask underlying disease
Mild reticulocytosis can be missed if smear not examined
Normal chest X‑ray early in acute chest syndrome
